entry: American hip-hop group from Compton, California. Active from 1987 to 1991, N.W.A (an abbreviation for Niggaz Wit Attitudes) was among the earliest and most significant figures of the gangsta rap subgenre. Its explicit lyrics drew controversy, and the group was banned from many mainstream American radio stations. Drawing on its members' experiences of [[Racism]] and excessive policing, its music was inherently political, and its accusations of institutional racism within the American police contributed to the political awareness of many American youth. Its debut album, *Straight Outta Compton* (1989), marked the start of the gangsta rap era, and *Niggaz4Life* (1991) was the first hardcore rap album to reach number one on the *Billboard* 200 sales chart. Members [[Eazy-E]], [[Ice Cube]] and [[Dr. Dre]] became platinum-selling solo artists. The group was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2016.

Shah of [[Iran]] (r. 1736–1747) and founder of the Afsharid dynasty. Born Nadr Qoli, he belonged to the Turkoman Afshars, one of seven Qizilbash tribes that helped the [[Safavid dynasty]] establish its power in Iran. He rose during a period of chaos after Hotaki Afghans overthrew the weak emperor Soltan Hoseyn. Nader reunited the Iranian realm, removed the [[Ottoman Empire]] and [[Russian Empire]] from its territory, and in 1736 deposed the last Safavids and declared himself shah. His campaigns, which included victories at [[Herat]] and Karnal, created an empire that at its maximum extent briefly encompassed all or part of modern-day Afghanistan, Georgia, India and Iraq, but his military spending ruined the economy. He idolized [[Genghis Khan]] and [[Timur]]. He was assassinated during a rebellion, after which his empire quickly disintegrated and Iran fell into civil war.

French music teacher, conductor and composer. Born into a musical family, the daughter of composer Ernest Boulanger, she entered the [[Paris]] Conservatoire at an early age but, believing she lacked compositional talent, turned to teaching. She taught many of the leading composers and musicians of the 20th century, especially those from the United States and other English-speaking countries. Her students included [[Aaron Copland]], [[Philip Glass]], [[Quincy Jones]], [[Astor Piazzolla]], Elliott Carter, Daniel Barenboim and Dinu Lipatti, and she taught over 250 others. Her principal base was her family flat in Paris, where she taught for most of the seven decades from the start of her career until her death at age 92. She was the first woman to conduct many major orchestras in America and Europe, including the [[BBC|BBC Symphony]], Boston Symphony, Hallé and Philadelphia orchestras, and she conducted several world premieres, including works by Copland and Stravinsky.

Romanian former gymnast. At the 1976 Summer Olympics in [[Montreal]], aged 14, she became the first gymnast to be awarded a perfect score of 10.0 at the [[Olympic Games]]. She earned six more perfect 10s at those Games and won three gold medals. At the 1980 Summer Olympics in [[Moscow]], she won two more gold medals and achieved two more perfect 10s. All five of her Olympic gold medals were in individual events, and she won nine Olympic medals and four World Artistic Gymnastics Championship medals in total. Praised for her artistry and grace, she brought unprecedented global popularity to the sport in the mid-1970s, and *El País* called her "the most iconic gymnast of the 20th century." In 1989 she defected from then-Communist [[Romania]], and she has lived in the United States since. She later married American Olympic gold medalist Bart Conner.

South African writer and political activist. Her writing dealt with moral and racial issues, particularly [[Apartheid|apartheid]] in South Africa, and works such as *Burger's Daughter* were banned under that regime. She joined the [[African National Congress]] while it was banned and gave [[Nelson Mandela]] advice on his 1964 defense speech at the trial that led to his life sentence. Born to Jewish immigrant parents near Springs, a mining town outside [[Johannesburg]], she began publishing as a child and moved to Johannesburg in 1948. She believed the [[Short story|short story]] was the literary form of her age, and she published many in *The New Yorker*. She received the [[Booker Prize]] for *The Conservationist* (1974) and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991. She later became active in [[HIV/AIDS]] causes.

State in northeastern India, with its capital at Kohima. The state's 17 major [[Tribe|tribes]] each differ in customs, language and dress, and the region has a rich tradition of [[Folklore|folklore]]. The Naga National Council, led by Zapu Phizo, demanded an independent Naga state and waged an armed insurgency. The state was formally inaugurated on December 1, 1963, as the 16th state of the Indian Union. It borders [[Assam]], [[Arunachal Pradesh]], [[Manipur]] and Myanmar. The primary sector, mostly agriculture, still accounts for 24.6% of the economy. The 2011 census recorded a population of 1,980,602, one of the least populated states in India.

Indian Mahāyāna Buddhist philosopher and monk, considered the founder of the Madhyamaka school. Regarded as the most important [[Buddhist philosophy|Buddhist philosopher]] after the [[The Buddha|Buddha]] himself, he is called the "second Buddha" in Tibetan Buddhism. His treatises are the foundational texts of the view of emptiness (Śūnyatāvāda), or Madhyamaka. His most important text, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (*Root Verses on Madhyamaka*), inspired commentaries in [[Sanskrit]], Chinese, Tibetan, Korean and Japanese and is still studied. His philosophy influenced [[Indian philosophy]] for a millennium and remains central to Mahāyāna Buddhism in East Asia and Tibet. Very little is reliably known of his life. Most scholars place him in South India, and some argue that he was an advisor to a king of the Sātavāhana dynasty, which ruled the [[Deccan Plateau]].

Port city and capital of Nagasaki Prefecture on the island of [[Kyushu]], Japan (pop., 2024: 392,281). Founded by the Portuguese, the port became the sole port for trade with the Portuguese and Dutch during the 16th through 19th centuries. Its Hidden Christian Sites were included in the UNESCO World Heritage List. In August 1945, three days after [[Hiroshima]], the United States dropped an atomic bomb on the city, making it the second city in the world to experience a nuclear attack, near the end of [[World War II]]. The city was later rebuilt.

Mountainous region of the southeastern Lesser Caucasus, within present-day [[Azerbaijan]]. Most of the region was governed by ethnic Armenians under the breakaway Republic of Artsakh, also called the Nagorno-Karabakh Republic, from the end of the first war with Azerbaijan in 1994 until the republic's dissolution was announced in September 2023. The region is usually equated with the former Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast of the [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] era, which covered 4,400 sq km. Its majority-Armenian population variously advocated independence or integration into [[Armenia]]. The Second Nagorno-Karabakh War began on September 27, 2020, and ended with a trilateral ceasefire on November 10, 2020. Azerbaijan regained territory surrounding the region and captured one-third of Nagorno-Karabakh, including Shusha and Hadrut. Azerbaijan launched a new offensive on September 19, 2023, and on January 1, 2024, the Republic of Artsakh was formally dissolved. Political analysts and residents accused Azerbaijan of ethnic cleansing, and the forced removal of almost the entire Armenian population followed.

Capital of Aichi Prefecture in central [[Honshu]], Japan (pop., 2025: 2.3 million). It is the largest city in the Chūbu region and the principal city of the Chūkyō metropolitan area, the third-most populous in Japan. Its seaport is the largest in Japan. In 1610 the shogun [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] moved the capital of Owari Province from Kiyosu to Nagoya, and Nagoya Castle was renovated during this period. From the [[Meiji Restoration]] the city grew rapidly as an industrial hub, with automobile, aviation and shipbuilding industries; these made it a target of American air raids during the [[Pacific War]]. After the war its economy diversified, and it is linked to [[Tokyo]], [[Osaka]] and [[Kyoto]] by the [[Shinkansen|Tokaido Shinkansen]]. The city hosts the 2026 Asian Games, the third Japanese city to do so after Tokyo (1958) and Hiroshima (1994).

Second capital and third-largest city of [[Maharashtra]], India. The largest and most populous city in central India, Nagpur is a major commercial and political center of the Vidarbha region, and the state assembly holds its annual winter session there. Founded in 1702 by the Gond king Bakht Buland Shah of Deogarh, it later became part of the [[Maratha Empire]] under the Bhonsle dynasty. The British [[East India Company]] took over the city in the 19th century and made it capital of the Central Provinces and Berar. Nagpur is known as the Orange City for its orange trade and as the Tiger Capital of India because many tiger reserves lie nearby. It is a key location of the Dalit Buddhist movement, and the Deekshabhoomi, the largest hollow stupa among the world's Buddhist stupas, is a major pilgrimage site. The city is also the headquarters of the right-wing Hindu nationalist [[Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh]].

Egyptian writer and Nobel laureate in literature (1988). Regarded as one of the first contemporary writers in Egyptian literature, along with Taha Hussein, to explore [[Existentialism|existentialism]], he was the only Egyptian to win the [[Nobel Prize]] in Literature. After studying philosophy at the Egyptian University, he joined the [[Civil service|civil service]] in 1934 and retired in 1971. He published 35 [[Novel|novels]], over 350 short stories, 26 screenplays and seven plays over a 70-year career, from the 1930s until 2004. All his novels are set in Egypt and mention "the lane" as a microcosm of the world. His most famous works include *The Cairo Trilogy* and *Children of Gebelawi*, and many of his works were adapted into Egyptian and international films.

Hard, protective plate at the tip of the [[Finger|fingers]] and toes of almost all [[Primate|primates]] (except marmosets), homologous to the claws of other [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]]. Fingernails and toenails are made of alpha-keratin, a tough rigid [[Protein|protein]] also found in the claws, hooves and horns of vertebrates. The nail matrix generates cells that harden as they move outward to form the nail plate, the visible hard part. The width and thickness of the plate depend on the matrix, and the shape of the fingertip bone determines whether it is flat, arched or hooked. The whitish crescent at the base, the lunula, is the visible part of the matrix. The nail plate contains no nerves or blood vessels, but the underlying nail bed is highly innervated, so removing the plate is often painful. The [[Cuticle]] is a layer of almost invisible dead skin covering the back of the plate.

Small, pointed fastener, usually of metal, used to join materials or to hang objects. Most nails have a sharp point and a flattened head, and the most common type is the wire nail. Other types include pins, tacks, brads, spikes and cleats. A nail holds materials together by friction in the axial direction and by shear strength laterally, and its point is sometimes bent over after driving to prevent pulling out. Nails are typically driven by a [[Hammer|hammer]] or nail gun. Until about 1800 artisans called nailers made nails by hand, and wire nails have been made since about 1860. At the time of the [[American Revolution]], [[England]] was the largest manufacturer of nails in the world. From the late 1700s to the mid-1900s, nail prices fell by a factor of 10.

Capital and largest city of [[Kenya]], in the south-central part of the country (pop., 2026: 5.6 million). Nicknamed the "Green City under the Sun," Nairobi is the only capital city in the world that hosts a national park within its boundaries. Its name comes from the Maasai phrase *Enkare Nyirobi*, meaning "place of cool waters." The city was founded in 1898 by colonial authorities as a rail depot on the Uganda–Kenya Railway, and it replaced [[Mombasa]] as Kenya's capital in 1907. After independence in 1963 it became the capital of the Republic of Kenya. During Kenya's early period it became a center for the [[Coffee|coffee]], [[Tea|tea]] and sisal industries. Nairobi is the major financial and economic hub of [[East Africa]]. The Nairobi Securities Exchange, one of the largest stock exchanges in Africa, is the continent's second-oldest. The city hosts the United Nations Office at Nairobi and the UN Environment Programme.

Any of several informal set theories used in the foundations of mathematics. Unlike axiomatic set theories, which are defined using formal logic, naive set theory is defined informally, in natural language. It describes sets as they are familiar from discrete mathematics, such as [[Venn diagram|Venn diagrams]] and reasoning about their [[Boolean algebra|Boolean algebra]], and it suffices for everyday use in contemporary mathematics. Most mathematical objects, including numbers, relations and functions, are defined in terms of sets. The first development of set theory was naive, created by [[Georg Cantor]] at the end of the 19th century. [[Gottlob Frege]] developed a formal but inconsistent system that led to [[Russell's paradox]]: there is no set consisting of all sets that do not contain themselves. Such paradoxes show that consistent set theories must limit the principles used to form sets, and [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] is one such axiomatic system.

Genus of venomous elapid snakes known as true cobras. Species occur throughout [[Africa]], Southwest Asia, [[South Asia]] and [[Southeast Asia]]. Several other elapids are called cobras, such as the [[King cobra]] and the rinkhals, but they are not true cobras because they do not belong to the genus. A 2009 revision merged the genera Boulengerina and Paranaja into Naja, bringing the total to 38 species, compared with 20 to 22 in earlier sources. The name derives from the [[Sanskrit]] *nāga*, meaning "snake." Most species have strongly neurotoxic [[Venom|venom]] that causes paralysis, though many also have cytotoxic features and a significant anticoagulant effect, and all species can deliver a fatal bite to a human. Several species, known as spitting cobras, eject venom forward from their fangs, which can cause blindness if it is not washed out of the eyes. The Caspian cobra (*N. oxiana*) of Central Asia is the most venomous Naja species.

Historical region of the [[Arabian Peninsula]] covering most of central [[Saudi Arabia]]. The name Najd means "highland" in Arabic. The region is divided into three provinces. Riyadh Province contains [[Riyadh]], the Saudi capital since 1824. Qassim Province is known for its fertile oases and [[Date palm|date palm]] orchards, and Ḥa'il Province features the mountains of Jabal Shammar. About one-third of Saudi Arabia's population lives in Najd. The House of Saud came from the region and pursued its unification with [[Hejaz]] from the time of the Emirate of Diriyah. The area's prehistory includes Al-Magar, a [[Neolithic]] culture in southwestern Najd that was possibly one of the first to practice widespread agriculture and animal domestication. Radiocarbon dating of its objects indicates an age of about 9,000 years.

Arabic term meaning "catastrophe" for the displacement of Palestinian Arabs in 1948. It describes the 1948 Palestine war, in which about 750,000 Palestinian Arabs, roughly half of [[Mandatory Palestine]]'s Arab population, were expelled or fled through violence, and over 500 Arab-majority towns and villages were depopulated. Palestinians regard the Nakba as a collective trauma that defines their national identity. Israelis regard the events as part of the War of Independence that established [[Israel]]. Critics describe the expulsions as ethnic cleansing, while historians remain divided on whether they were premeditated or the product of wartime conditions.

Burrowing eusocial rodent native to the [[Horn of Africa]] and parts of [[Kenya]]. Typical adults are 8 to 10 cm long and weigh 30 to 35 grams. It is the only mammalian thermoconformer, relying on an almost entirely ectothermic form of [[Thermoregulation|temperature regulation]]. Colonies show a reproductive division of labor, and the species has very low [[Metabolism|metabolic]] and respiratory rates. It survives for at least five hours in air containing only 5% [[Oxygen|oxygen]] and lacks pain sensitivity in its skin. The naked mole-rat is notable for its longevity and resistance to cancer.

[[Opioid]] antagonist sold under the brand name Narcan, among others. Naloxone reverses opioid effects and is commonly used to restore breathing after an overdose. It takes effect within two minutes when given intravenously and within about ten minutes as a nasal spray, and it blocks opioid effects for 30 to 90 minutes, so longer-acting opioids may need repeated doses. Administration to opioid-dependent people may cause withdrawal symptoms. Naloxone was patented in 1961 and approved for opioid overdose in the United States in 1971. It is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines and is available over the counter.

Word or words used for identification by an external observer. A name can identify a class of things or a single thing, uniquely or within a given context. A [[Personal name|personal name]] identifies, not necessarily uniquely, a specific human. The name of a specific entity is a proper name, and a one-word proper name is a proper noun. In most of Europe and the Americas the given name comes before the [[Surname|surname]], but in parts of Asia and [[Hungary]] the surname comes first. Products and courses follow naming conventions, and automobiles typically have a make and a model. In biology, [[Binomial nomenclature|binomial nomenclature]] gives species two-part names. The word comes from [[Old English]] *nama*.

headword: Names of the days of the week
sort_key: names of the days of the week
entry: Labels for the seven days of the week, derived in many languages from the classical planets. The planetary system was introduced by the [[Sumer|Sumerians]] and adopted by the [[Roman Empire]] in late antiquity. In some languages, including English, the days instead take their names from regional deities, such as the Germanic gods reflected in the English weekdays. The seven-day week was adopted in early Christianity from the Hebrew calendar, and Emperor Constantine made it official in AD 321. [[Sunday]] remained the first day of the week, while the Jewish [[Sabbath]] remained the seventh. Under ISO 8601, [[Monday]] is the first day.

Country in southern Africa, officially a republic (pop., 3.1 million). Its capital and largest city is [[Windhoek]], and it is the driest country in sub-Saharan Africa. Bantu peoples arrived around the 14th century. In 1884 the [[German Empire]] established rule over most of the territory, and between 1904 and 1908 German troops waged a campaign against the Herero and Nama that escalated into the first genocide of the 20th century. The [[League of Nations]] mandated administration to South Africa in 1920, and apartheid was applied after the National Party took power in 1948. Namibia gained independence in March 1990, though Walvis Bay and the Penguin Islands remained under South African control until 1994. Agriculture, tourism and mining form the basis of the economy, and income inequality is among the world's highest, with a [[Gini coefficient]] of 59 in 2015. Namibia is a member of the [[United Nations]] and the [[African Union]].

Rapid transit system serving [[Bengaluru]], the capital of [[Karnataka]], India. It is the second-largest metro network in India, behind [[Delhi Metro]] as of November 2026, with an operational length of 103.6 km. Of its 91 operational stations as of November 2026, 83 are elevated, seven are underground and one is at grade. The system is powered by 750V direct current through a third rail. It opened in 2011 as the first metro in South India and in 2016 became the first underground metro in South India. It is operated by a joint venture of the [[Government of India]] and the government of Karnataka.
